paragraphs: By train, the most direct option for the university is the FGC R5 line from Barcelona-Plaça Espanya to Manresa-Baixador, the stop UManresa recommends. From there it is a few minutes' walk to QEhome.

With Renfe, the R4 (Rodalies) and R12 (regional) lines arrive at Manresa station, in the lower part of town by the Cardener river. From there to the apartment it is best to take a taxi or allow for a longer walk.
By car from Barcelona, take the C-16 (toll) or the A-2 and C-55 (toll-free), around an hour. From El Prat airport the drive takes about the same; by public transport you need to change in Barcelona.

queVerPage.h1: What to see in Manresa: a guide to the city in 1 or 2 days
queVerPage.heroSubtitle: Manresa has enough heritage, history and surroundings to deserve more than a few hours. This guide covers the places most worth seeing and a simple route for one or two days.

items.label: Must-sees
items.value: La Seu and the Cave of Saint Ignatius

items.label: Time needed
items.value: 1 full day, or 2 with a day trip

items.label: From QEhome
items.value: Plaça Major about 20 min on foot

items.label: Main festival

sections.title: What to see in Manresa: the essentials
paragraphs: If you are looking for what to see in Manresa, these are the points a first visit usually starts with.

subsections.title: La Seu de Manresa
paragraphs: The Basilica of Santa Maria de Manresa, known as La Seu, is the city's main monumental landmark and one of the standout examples of Catalan Gothic.
The present building began in 1328 to designs by Berenguer de Montagut, also linked to Santa Maria del Mar in Barcelona. Alongside the architecture, it holds important works of art inside.
Tip: it is a good place to start. From the Seu area you walk straight into the historic core.

subsections.title: The Cave of Saint Ignatius
paragraphs: The Cave of Saint Ignatius is one of Manresa's best-known places internationally.

Ignatius of Loyola spent a long period in the city in 1522. Tradition places part of his spiritual experience and the origins of the Spiritual Exercises in this cave. Over time the natural shelter became the present sanctuary, with views over the Cardener and towards Montserrat.
It is worth visiting for its religious significance, the architectural complex and its position above the valley.

subsections.title: The historic centre and Plaça Major
paragraphs: Old Manresa still keeps the structure of the medieval city.

From La Seu you can walk to Plaça Major, streets such as Sant Miquel and Sobrerroca, Plana de l'Om and other historic routes. Manresa Tourism identifies this core as one of the city's main heritage areas.
It is a place to wander without heavy planning: much of the interest comes from linking streets, squares and buildings.

subsections.title: Carrer del Balç
paragraphs: Carrer del Balç is one of the best places to imagine medieval Manresa.
It is a narrow, winding street, partly covered by structures built between the houses in the Middle Ages. The interpretation centre explains the fourteenth-century city with audiovisual materials.
Important: Manresa Tourism currently lists the centre as temporarily closed for accessibility works. Check its status before you go.

subsections.title: Museu del Barroc de Catalunya
paragraphs: The Museu del Barroc de Catalunya is housed in the former College of Saint Ignatius and brings together around 200 works of painting, sculpture, altarpieces and decorative arts from the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.
It is not only a local museum: it is presented as a reference centre for Catalan Baroque. If you have more than a few hours in Manresa, it deserves a place among the main visits.

subsections.title: Pont Vell and the River Cardener
paragraphs: Pont Vell crosses the Cardener at the foot of the historic centre and forms part of Manresa's monumental image.

The route from La Seu to Pont Vell and the Cave of Saint Ignatius is one of the most visually rewarding in the city. This area also helps explain why the Cardener landscape is so closely tied to Ignatius's stay in Manresa.

subsections.title: Passeig Pere III and the modern centre
paragraphs: After the medieval and Ignatian heritage, it is worth walking Manresa's more urban axis.
Passeig Pere III is the city's main boulevard. It links shopping areas and buildings from modern Manresa's growth. It is a good place to eat, have a drink or finish a walk through the centre.

sections.title: Manresa in half a day
paragraphs: If you only have a few hours, prioritise this route: La Seu, Plaça Major and the historic centre, Pont Vell and the Cave of Saint Ignatius.
It is a clear way to get a first impression without trying to see everything. It combines the three main strands: medieval, Ignatian and the Cardener landscape.

sections.title: What to see in Manresa in one day
paragraphs: With a full day you can widen the route without packing the schedule too tightly.

subsections.title: Morning
paragraphs: Start at La Seu, the city's main monument. Continue towards Plaça Major, Sobrerroca and Plana de l'Om.
If Carrer del Balç is open on your dates, it is one of the best places to understand medieval Manresa. It is currently listed as temporarily closed for works; check the status before you go.

Keep part of the morning or midday for the Museu del Barroc. Usual published hours: Tuesday to Saturday 10:00 to 18:00, and Sundays and public holidays 10:00 to 15:00. Always confirm official hours before visiting.

subsections.title: Lunch
paragraphs: For lunch, the centre and Passeig Pere III concentrate much of the offer. We will publish a concrete shortlist later; for now, choose according to timing and preference.

subsections.title: Afternoon
paragraphs: Head down to the Cardener via Pont Vell. Leave time for the Cave of Saint Ignatius and its surroundings. Finish the day on Passeig Pere III or in the city centre.

sections.title: If you have two days in Manresa
paragraphs: The second day does not have to be an automatic trip out of town. You can keep exploring the city or head into the surrounding area.

subsections.title: Option A: keep discovering Manresa
paragraphs: Parc de l'Agulla: one of the city's main open spaces. Its lake covers about 64,000 m² and forms part of the water system linked to the historic Séquia de Manresa. There are green areas, services and leisure spaces. It works especially well for families or if you want a break from urban heritage.
Parc de la Séquia: the medieval canal is one of the most important elements in Manresa's history. Today it also forms part of nature and heritage routes.

Modernista heritage: Manresa also keeps Modernista and industrial architecture. Often-cited examples include Casa Torrents, Torre Lluvià and La Florinda. They show a Manresa beyond the purely medieval or Ignatian story.

subsections.title: Option B: a day trip from Manresa
paragraphs: [[Montserrat|visitar-montserrat-desde-manresa]] is the clearest day trip to combine with a stay in Manresa.
[[Wine tourism in Pla de Bages|enoturismo-pla-de-bages]] offers wine, landscape and wineries nearby.
Món Sant Benet can also work for heritage and food in the Bages area. Manresa Tourism includes it among the main attractions of the surrounding area.

sections.title: What to see in Manresa with children
paragraphs: If you visit Manresa as a family, not everything has to be historic heritage. Parc de l'Agulla offers open space and a play area. Some cultural venues run family activities on specific dates; check the official agenda.

sections.title: Manresa and Ignatius of Loyola
paragraphs: The link between Manresa and Ignatius of Loyola sets the city apart from many inland Catalan destinations. Ignatius stayed here for about eleven months from 1522, and the city still has many places tied to that stay. Manresa Tourism currently identifies 22 Ignatian sites. If you arrive on the [[Ignatian Way|alojamiento-camino-ignaciano-manresa]], Manresa is the historic end of the route.
For a first visit, the most useful stops are usually the Cave of Saint Ignatius, La Seu, Espai Manresa 1522, Pou de la Gallina and spaces of the former Hospital of Santa Llúcia.

sections.title: Festivals and events in Manresa
paragraphs: Some dates change the feel of the city completely. If you can choose when to come, these are the best-known events:
items: Festa de la Llum (February): Manresa's main traditional festival, around 21 February, commemorating the 1345 legend of the light linked to the Séquia canal.
Fira de l'Aixada (February): a medieval market and re-enactment in the streets of the old town, coinciding with the Festa de la Llum.
Festa Major (late August): concerts, folk culture and events across the city.
Fira Mediterrània (autumn): one of Catalonia's leading performing arts and folk culture markets, with shows in the streets and theatres.
sections.tip: During festivals occupancy rises and parking in the centre gets harder. If you are driving, booking with a parking space included saves you looking for one.

sections.title: Practical tips for visiting Manresa
paragraphs: Getting around: the historic centre and most of the main sights are walkable. For Parc de l'Agulla or trips into the Bages, a car is often more practical.

Arriving by train: Manresa has FGC and Renfe connections. Manresa Tourism cites FGC lines R5 and R50, and Renfe lines R4 and R12. We do not give fixed journey times because timetables and services can change.

Opening hours: for museums, monuments and visitor sites, always check official pages before you go. This matters especially for places such as Carrer del Balç, which is currently listed as temporarily closed.
If you arrive by car, QEhome has [[private parking and an electric car charger|apartamento-parking-manresa]].
For a half-day trip, [[Cardona and its Salt Mountain|visitar-cardona-desde-manresa]] is about 35 minutes away by car.

faqs.q: How many days do you need to see Manresa?
faqs.a: One full day covers the essentials: La Seu, the old town, the Museu del Barroc, the Pont Vell and the Cave of Saint Ignatius. With two days you can add Parc de l'Agulla, the modernista buildings or a trip to Montserrat.

faqs.q: Can you explore Manresa on foot?
faqs.a: Yes. The old town and main monuments are within walking distance. For Parc de l'Agulla or trips around the Bages, a car is more practical.

faqs.q: How do you get to Manresa from Barcelona?
faqs.a: By train with FGC (R5 and R50 from Plaça Espanya) or Renfe (R4 and R12), or by car on the C-16 or C-55, around an hour.

faqs.q: What is Manresa best known for?
faqs.a: La Seu, the Gothic basilica that dominates the skyline, and the Cave of Saint Ignatius, linked to Ignatius of Loyola's stay in 1522.

sections.title: Manresa, end of the Ignatian Way
paragraphs: The Ignatian Way reaches Manresa, a city linked to Saint Ignatius's stay and the [[Cave of Saint Ignatius|que-ver-manresa]]. For many pilgrims the route ends here, or it is a long stage before continuing.
In the centre you have services, shops and Ignatian heritage a short walk away. QEhome is on Carrer Doctor Esteve, near Manresa-Baixador FGC station.

sections.title: The Ignatian Way in brief
paragraphs: The Ignatian Way retraces the journey Ignatius of Loyola made in 1522 from his birthplace in Loyola (Azpeitia, Gipuzkoa) to Manresa. It covers about 650 km in 27 stages through the Basque Country, La Rioja, Navarre, Aragon and Catalonia.
Many pilgrims do not walk the whole route: it is common to do only the Catalan section, from Lleida or from Montserrat, and finish in Manresa with a visit to the Cave of Saint Ignatius.

sections.title: The final stage: Montserrat to Manresa
paragraphs: The last stage leaves Montserrat monastery and reaches Manresa after about 25-26 km, according to the route published by Manresa Tourism. It is a long day with significant elevation changes, so start early.

In summer the heat is strong on the unshaded sections: carry enough water and sun protection. If you want to spend the night before in Montserrat, our guide to [[Montserrat from Manresa|visitar-montserrat-desde-manresa]] will help you plan the visit.

sections.title: When you arrive in Manresa
paragraphs: The Pilgrim Welcome Centre is at Via Sant Ignasi, 40 (ground floor of the old Saint Ignatius college). You can stamp your credential there. Usual hours: 10:00 to 18:00, Monday to Sunday. Closed on 25 and 26 December and on 1 and 6 January.
The Ignatian Way certificate (Ignaciana) can be collected at the Manresa Tourist Office on Plaça Major, with a credential stamped according to the route requirements.
If you arrive outside Welcome Centre hours, you can stamp the next day. At QEhome check-in is self-service: you do not need a front desk to shower and rest.

Full kitchen for dinner or breakfast without going out. Full bathroom. Two bedrooms if you travel as a couple or a small group. WiFi. If you arrive by car, private parking in the building.

sections.title: Getting home from Manresa
paragraphs: Both FGC and Renfe run trains from Manresa to Barcelona. The FGC R5 leaves from Manresa-Baixador, close to QEhome, and arrives at Barcelona-Plaça Espanya. Renfe's R4 and R12 leave from Manresa station, in the lower part of town; the R12 also runs to Lleida.
To catch a flight from Barcelona-El Prat you need to change in Barcelona. If someone is picking you up by car, they can park in the building's private space.

sections.title: If you travel with a support car
paragraphs: Some groups walk the Way with a vehicle carrying luggage or picking up whoever needs a rest. At QEhome the car stays in the [[building's private car park|apartamento-parking-manresa]], with a lift straight to the flat for rucksacks and suitcases.

sections.title: If you stay an extra day
paragraphs: With one more night you can take your time over the Ignatian sites and the old town: our guide to [[what to see in Manresa|que-ver-manresa]] covers La Seu, the Pont Vell, the Cave and the city's 22 Ignatian sites.
If you reached Manresa without passing through Montserrat, you can also go back to the mountain by train or car and return to sleep in the same apartment.

sections.title: Why visit Montserrat from Manresa?
paragraphs: Montserrat is one of Catalonia's best-known day trips and combines well with a stay in Manresa.

From Manresa you can organise a half-day or full-day outing and return to the city afterwards, without changing accommodation. If you also want to explore the city, see [[what to see in Manresa|que-ver-manresa]].
Information reviewed in September 2026. Opening hours, transport and services at Montserrat can change: always check the official website before you leave.

sections.title: How to get to Montserrat from Manresa
paragraphs: You can go by car or by train. The best option depends on whether you want to park in Monistrol, drive up to the monastery or travel only by public transport.

subsections.title: By car
paragraphs: From Manresa the road takes you towards Monistrol de Montserrat. From there you can drive up to the monastery area, park in Monistrol and take the rack railway (Cremallera), or go to the Aeri access and take the cable car.
We do not give a fixed journey time because it varies with traffic, your exact starting point and which Montserrat access you choose.

subsections.title: By train
paragraphs: FGC line R5 links Manresa with the Montserrat access stations for both the Cremallera and the Aeri. The official Montserrat website notes that trains from Manresa connect with both systems.
This is useful if you are not travelling by car or prefer not to park on the mountain.

sections.title: Cremallera or Aeri: which to choose
paragraphs: Both systems take you from the base up to the monastery. The choice usually depends on where you park or which FGC station you use.

subsections.title: Montserrat rack railway (Cremallera)
paragraphs: The Cremallera connects Monistrol de Montserrat with the monastery in about 15 minutes. The usual frequency from Monistrol Vila is about every 20 minutes. Its station has free parking for around 900 cars, according to official information.

subsections.title: Montserrat cable car (Aeri)
paragraphs: The cable car takes about 5 minutes and usually runs roughly every 15 minutes. There is also free parking at the lower station, according to official information.

sections.title: What to see at Montserrat
paragraphs: You do not need to see everything. These are the clearest stops for a first visit.

subsections.title: Basilica of Santa Maria de Montserrat
paragraphs: The basilica is the spiritual centre of the sanctuary. It houses the image of Our Lady of Montserrat, known as La Moreneta, a twelfth-century Romanesque carving.

subsections.title: La Moreneta
paragraphs: Visiting the Virgin's chapel is one of the most emblematic moments. The official website publishes separate hours for access to the throne; check them on the day of your visit.

subsections.title: Montserrat Museum
paragraphs: The museum holds collections of old and modern painting, archaeology, iconography and religious art. It is one of the main cultural attractions on the site.

subsections.title: Santa Cova
paragraphs: According to tradition, this is where the image of the Virgin was found. The path also includes the Monumental Rosary, with important Modernista works.

subsections.title: Sant Joan funicular and viewpoints
paragraphs: When it is running, it takes you up to Pla de les Taràntules for panoramic views and mountain walks. Check beforehand whether it is in service.

subsections.title: Hiking
paragraphs: Montserrat offers walks from the monastery and harder routes such as the one towards Sant Jeroni. The official website describes a route of about 7 km and around 2 hours 30 minutes from the Sant Joan area. It only makes sense if you have time, fitness and good weather.

sections.title: Half-day route
paragraphs: If you only have a few hours, focus on the monastery without long hikes.
items: Monastery
Basilica and La Moreneta

Museum or a short walk

sections.title: Full-day route
paragraphs: With a full day you can widen the visit without trying to cover every mountain route.

subsections.title: Morning
paragraphs: Arrive early. Basilica, La Moreneta and the Montserrat Museum.

subsections.title: Midday
paragraphs: Lunch on site or a picnic if that suits you. Check café and service hours on the official website.

subsections.title: Afternoon
paragraphs: Choose Santa Cova or, if it is running, Sant Joan and a short walk. Then return to Manresa.

sections.title: What to check before you go
paragraphs: Before leaving, check the official Montserrat website for the status of the funiculars, basilica hours, access to the Virgin's throne, the museum and ticket or service availability.

sections.title: Montserrat with children
paragraphs: For families, the monastery, viewpoints, the audiovisual space and short walks are usually easier than long mountain routes.
Montserrat's educational offer includes nature and funicular activities for children and schools when those services are available.

sections.title: Montserrat and Ignatius of Loyola
paragraphs: Montserrat and Manresa are linked on the Ignatian Way. The final official stage runs from Montserrat to Manresa, about 25 to 26 km according to the route published by Manresa Tourism.
If you are walking the route, Manresa is the natural arrival point after Montserrat.
If you have another day, [[Cardona and its Salt Mountain|visitar-cardona-desde-manresa]] is about 35 minutes from Manresa on the C-55.

faqs.q: How long does it take from Manresa to Montserrat?
faqs.a: By car, about 25 minutes to Monistrol for the rack railway or cable car, and 35-40 minutes if you drive up to the monastery. By train, the FGC R5 connects with both.

faqs.q: Do you have to pay to enter the basilica?
faqs.a: Entry to the basilica is free. The museum, funiculars, rack railway and cable car are paid. Check prices on the official website.

faqs.q: Rack railway or cable car?
faqs.a: The cable car is quicker (about 5 minutes) and more spectacular; the rack railway takes about 15 minutes and has a large car park in Monistrol. It mainly depends on where you park or which FGC station you use.

faqs.a: Yes. That is one of the advantages of staying in Manresa: leave in the morning, visit Montserrat and come back to sleep in the same place without changing accommodation.

sections.title: Why stay in Manresa to visit Pla de Bages
paragraphs: Pla de Bages is a wine designation with family wineries, vineyards and landscape a short drive from Manresa. The wine route works best by car: booked visits, tastings and a return to town for dinner or rest.
QEhome is not a rural house among vineyards. It is an urban apartment with private parking and an electric car charger: go out to wineries by day and return to the centre.

sections.title: What is the DO Pla de Bages
paragraphs: The DO Pla de Bages is one of Catalonia's smallest wine appellations. It covers the plain around Manresa, with vineyards among woodland and farmhouses and Montserrat and Sant Llorenç del Munt on the horizon.

In the 19th century the Bages was one of the most heavily planted wine areas in Catalonia, until phylloxera wiped out the vineyards at the end of the century. Recovery came much later, led by family wineries focused on small production and local varieties.

The grape that sets the area apart is white Picapoll, almost exclusive to the Bages, which makes fresh, aromatic whites. Macabeo and Chardonnay are also grown, along with reds such as Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Ull de Llebre (Tempranillo), Garnacha and the revived Sumoll.

sections.title: Vineyard 'tines': a unique heritage
paragraphs: Tines are dry-stone structures built in the middle of the vineyards so the grapes could be fermented on the spot rather than carted back to the village. Most date from the 18th and 19th centuries and are one of the defining features of the Bages wine landscape.

Some particularly well-preserved groups are in the Vall del Flequer, between Mura and Talamanca, inside Sant Llorenç del Munt i l'Obac Natural Park. Waymarked walking routes visit them and pair well with a morning at a winery.

sections.title: When to go
paragraphs: The harvest, from late August into September, is the busiest time: some wineries run special days and you can see the work in the vineyards. Spring and autumn are pleasant for temperature and scenery.
In summer, schedule visits early in the morning or late afternoon. In winter there is less on offer, but booked visits tend to be quieter.

sections.title: Tips for planning your visit
items: Always book ahead: most wineries only open for pre-arranged visits with limited places.
Ask whether the visit includes the vineyard and a tasting, and how long it lasts, so you can fit two wineries into one day without rushing.
Choose a designated driver or keep drives short: the nearest wineries are 10-15 minutes from Manresa.
Wear comfortable shoes if the visit includes a walk through the vineyards or to the tines.
If you buy wine, the car boot stays in the building's [[private car park|apartamento-parking-manresa]] rather than on the street.

sections.title: Món Sant Benet and food
paragraphs: About 15 minutes from Manresa, Món Sant Benet combines a medieval monastery with a Romanesque cloister and a space devoted to cooking and food. It works well alongside a winery route, especially in bad weather or with children.

sections.title: More ideas nearby

faqs.q: Do I need to book to visit Pla de Bages wineries?
faqs.a: In practice, almost always. Most wineries work with pre-arranged visits and limited places; check their websites or the DO Pla de Bages Wine Route.

faqs.q: What wine is typical of the Bages?
faqs.a: White Picapoll, a variety almost exclusive to the area. There are also good reds from Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon and Sumoll.

faqs.q: Can I do the route without a car?
faqs.a: It is difficult: public transport to the wineries is limited. The ones closest to Manresa, such as Oller del Mas, are a short taxi ride away.

faqs.q: When is the harvest?
faqs.a: Usually from late August into September, depending on the variety and the vintage.

cardonaPage.h1: Visiting Cardona from Manresa: Salt Mountain and castle
cardonaPage.heroSubtitle: A half-day or full-day trip about 35 minutes from Manresa: the old salt mine, the castle with the collegiate church of Sant Vicenç, and the old town.

items.label: Distance
items.value: About 31 km · 35 min on the C-55

items.label: Time
items.value: Half a day or a full day

sections.title: Why visit Cardona
paragraphs: Cardona brings together two of the most unusual places in Catalonia in a single town: a mountain of salt that has been worked for thousands of years and a medieval fortress overlooking the Cardener valley.

From Manresa it is one of the easiest trips to plan: you get there in just over half an hour and can be back to sleep in the same apartment. It pairs well with a visit to [[Montserrat|visitar-montserrat-desde-manresa]] or a day in [[Manresa|que-ver-manresa]].

subsections.title: By car
paragraphs: Take the C-55 towards Solsona, up the Cardener valley and through Súria. It is about 31 km and about 35 minutes from QEhome. This is the easiest option for combining the mine and the castle, which are at opposite ends of town.

subsections.title: By bus
paragraphs: There are intercity buses between Manresa and Cardona. Check times and frequency before you set off, especially at weekends, when the service is more limited.

sections.title: The Salt Mountain
paragraphs: The Muntanya de Sal is an outcrop of salt that reaches the surface beside the river Cardener. Cardona's salt has been used since prehistoric times and for centuries was the great source of wealth of the lords of Cardona. In the 20th century it was worked as a potash mine until it closed.
Today the Muntanya de Sal Cultural Park runs guided tours inside the old mine: galleries dug into the salt, salt formations and an explanation of how people worked underground.
sections.tip: Book the mine tour in advance in high season and at weekends, and check the minimum age if you're going with young children. Wear comfortable shoes.

sections.title: The castle and the collegiate church of Sant Vicenç
paragraphs: Above the town stands Cardona Castle, one of the most important medieval fortresses in Catalonia and the former residence of the Dukes of Cardona. Today it houses a Parador hotel, but the site can be visited.

Inside the walls is the collegiate church of Sant Vicenç, consecrated in the 11th century and considered one of the key works of Lombard Romanesque in Catalonia. From the walls there are views over the town and the Salt Mountain.

sections.title: Cardona's old town
paragraphs: Between the mine and the castle it is worth walking the streets of the old town, with Plaça de la Fira and the Gothic church of Sant Miquel. It is a small area you can cover on foot quickly, and it is where most places to eat are.

sections.title: A day trip from Manresa
items: Morning: leave Manresa and take the guided tour of the Salt Mountain.
Midday: lunch in Cardona's old town.
Afternoon: castle, collegiate church of Sant Vicenç and views from the walls.
Return: back to Manresa on the C-55; if there's time, stop in Súria's old quarter.

sections.title: Cardona with kids
paragraphs: The mine is one of the outings children enjoy most in the area: going inside a mountain of salt is hard to forget. The castle, with its walls and towers, rounds off the day nicely.

For families, it's best to start with the mine in the morning and leave the castle for the afternoon, without trying to squeeze in more visits. More ideas on the [[family apartment|apartamento-familias-manresa]] page.

sections.title: Tips and what to combine
items: Check opening times and bookings on the official Salt Mountain and castle websites before you go.
If you have time left, Solsona is about 20 minutes further north on the C-55.
For a full weekend: one day in Cardona, another in [[Montserrat|visitar-montserrat-desde-manresa]] and an afternoon in central Manresa.
When you get back, the car goes in the [[private parking|apartamento-parking-manresa]] in QEhome's building.

faqs.q: How long does it take from Manresa to Cardona?
faqs.a: About 35 minutes by car on the C-55, roughly 31 km. There are also intercity buses.

faqs.q: Can you visit the salt mine with children?
faqs.a: Yes, it is a very popular visit with families. Check the minimum age and book ahead at weekends.

faqs.q: Is there time to see the mine and the castle in one day?
faqs.a: Yes. With the mine in the morning, lunch in town and the castle in the afternoon, you see the essentials without rushing.

faqs.q: What else is there to see near Cardona?
faqs.a: Solsona is about 20 minutes north, and on the way back to Manresa you can stop in Súria.
